articles.label: Analysis
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47M reserve fund sits untouched as commissioners debate hurricane prep spending
articles.dek: Three budget workshops in and no one can agree on what counts as an emergency. Meanwhile, forecasters predict an above-average Atlantic season.
brief: Escambia County holds $47.2 million in unassigned reserves while commissioners disagree on criteria for pre-storm spending
Three budget workshops have produced no consensus on emergency fund disbursement policies ahead of peak hurricane season
NOAA predicts 17-21 named storms this season; county's drainage infrastructure still recovering from 2024 damage
articles.body:
The projector in Room 100 of the Ernie Lee Magaha Government Building flickered Tuesday morning as County Administrator Wes Moreno pulled up the same spreadsheet commissioners had seen twice before. Forty-seven point two million dollars in unassigned general fund reserves. A number that hasn't moved since April.

"We're not here to relitigate the reserve policy," Commissioner Jeff Bergosh said before anyone else could speak. "We're here to talk about the drainage master plan."

But that's exactly where the conversation went anyway. For the third consecutive budget workshop, Escambia County commissioners spent more time debating when to spend emergency reserves than how to spend them. Peak hurricane season arrives in six weeks. The drainage infrastructure they're supposed to be discussing still carries damage from storms two years ago.

The policy vacuum

Escambia County maintains what it calls a "rainy day fund" — reserves equal to roughly two months of operating expenses. The money exists for emergencies. The problem is definitional.

"We don't have a written policy that defines what triggers a reserve disbursement," said Budget Director Sarah Chen during Tuesday's workshop. "We have historical practice and board discretion."

Historical practice, according to county records reviewed by The Flightline, means waiting until after a federally declared disaster to tap reserves. The county then uses reserve funds to cover expenses while awaiting FEMA reimbursement — a process that took 18 months following Hurricane Sally in 2020 and is still ongoing for some 2024 storm damage.

Commissioner Steven Barry has pushed for a different approach. At the June 24 workshop, he proposed authorizing $8 million in pre-storm drainage improvements, arguing the work would reduce post-storm costs.

"We're going to spend this money either way," Barry said then. "We can spend it fixing problems before they become disasters, or we can spend more fixing them after."

The motion died for lack of a second.

The drainage question

County Public Works Director Tom Nichols presented the drainage master plan update Tuesday for the fourth time in six months. The document identifies $156 million in needed improvements across unincorporated Escambia County. Priority projects total $43 million.

Nine of those priority projects sit in flood-prone areas that saw significant damage during the unnamed storm system that stalled over the county in August 2024. Four remain incomplete.

"We've done what we can with budgeted funds," Nichols said. "The Scenic Heights outfall project is 60% complete. Brownsville drainage is at maybe 40%. The others are in design."

When Commissioner Lumon May asked about timeline for completion, Nichols paused.

"If we stay on current funding trajectory, we're looking at FY 2029 for the priority list," he said. "That assumes no major storm events requiring emergency repairs."

The room went quiet.

The forecast

NOAA's updated Atlantic hurricane season outlook, released July 10, predicts 17 to 21 named storms, with eight to 11 becoming hurricanes. Four to six of those could reach major hurricane status — Category 3 or higher.

The National Weather Service in Mobile, which covers Escambia County, has classified 2026 as a "heightened risk" season for the central Gulf Coast. Sea surface temperatures in the Gulf of Mexico are running 1.5 to 2 degrees Fahrenheit above the 30-year average.

"Warmer water means more fuel for storms that enter the Gulf," said David Easterling, a meteorologist with NWS Mobile, in a phone interview. "We're not predicting specific impacts for specific locations. But the ingredients are there for an active season."

Escambia County's Emergency Management Division has updated its hurricane response plan and conducted two tabletop exercises since May, according to department records. The exercises assumed scenarios where drainage systems were "fully functional."

Where commissioners stand

The five-member board appears split, though no formal votes have occurred.

Bergosh, who represents District 1, has consistently argued for maintaining reserves at current levels until a declared emergency. At Tuesday's workshop, he cited the county's bond rating and the need for fiscal prudence.

"We don't spend emergency money on non-emergencies," he said. "That's not complicated."

Barry, representing District 4, countered that the definition of emergency was itself the question.

"If we know a storm is coming and we know our drainage can't handle it, is that not an emergency?" he asked. "Or do we wait until people's houses flood?"

May, from District 3, has not committed to either position publicly but asked staff Tuesday to model scenarios: What would drainage system performance look like in a 10-inch rain event with current infrastructure versus completed priority projects?

Nichols said he could have that analysis ready for the August 4 budget workshop.

Commissioner Mike Kohler, District 2, was absent Tuesday for a prior commitment. Commissioner Robert Bender, District 5, asked questions about FEMA reimbursement rates but did not indicate how he would vote on a reserve disbursement.

The math

The county's current reserve balance of $47.2 million equals 16.4% of the general fund operating budget. The county's informal policy targets 15% minimum reserves. Spending $8 million on drainage — Barry's proposal — would drop reserves to 13.6%.

Chen noted that the county's actual reserve target has never been formally adopted by the commission. The 15% figure appears in internal planning documents but not in any resolution or ordinance.

"We've operated on institutional knowledge," Chen said. "That's worked. But it does create ambiguity when the board considers non-traditional reserve uses."

Bergosh asked Chen whether the county could create an explicit reserve policy before the August workshops concluded. Chen said yes — if the board provided direction on what that policy should contain.

No direction was given.

What happens next

The next budget workshop is scheduled for August 4 at 9 a.m. in Room 100 of the Ernie Lee Magaha Government Building. The drainage master plan is on the agenda again, along with Nichols' scenario analysis.

Public comment is allowed at budget workshops but limited to three minutes per speaker. As of Tuesday afternoon, no members of the public had signed up to speak.

Peak hurricane season runs from mid-August through mid-October. The statistical peak for Gulf Coast landfalls is September 10.

The $47.2 million sits in an interest-bearing account at Hancock Whitney Bank, earning approximately 4.8% annually. At current rates, the county earns roughly $188,000 per month in interest on idle reserves.

Commissioner Barry, leaving the workshop Tuesday, stopped in the hallway.

"We'll be back here in two weeks having the same conversation," he said. "Maybe with a storm in the Gulf. Maybe not. But we'll be having it."

articles.label: Housing
articles.headline: The last mobile home park on Pensacola Beach faces a September deadline
articles.dek: Residents of Via de Luna trailer court have 60 days to relocate. Most have lived there for decades. None have found affordable alternatives on the island.
brief: Twelve households at Via de Luna trailer court must vacate by September 19 after the Santa Rosa Island Authority approved a lease transfer to Gulf Coast Development Partners
Residents, some of whom have lived on the site for over 30 years, say they cannot find comparable housing on the island for less than three times their current rent
The 2.1-acre parcel will become a mixed-use development with vacation rentals and retail space, continuing a decades-long trend of workforce housing elimination on the beach
articles.body:
The wind chimes on Dolores Hutchins' porch haven't stopped moving all morning. She sits in a lawn chair under the aluminum awning she installed herself in 1994, watching the traffic roll past on Via de Luna Drive. In 60 days, she will have to take the wind chimes down. She has nowhere to put them.

"I moved here when my husband was stationed at the base," Hutchins said. "He's been gone eleven years now. This is the only home I've got."

Hutchins is one of twelve households living at the Via de Luna trailer court, a 2.1-acre rectangle of crushed shell and concrete pads tucked behind a row of condominiums a half-mile east of the Pensacola Beach fishing pier. On May 22, the Santa Rosa Island Authority voted 4-1 to approve a lease transfer that will deliver the land to Gulf Coast Development Partners, a Destin-based firm that plans to build vacation rental units and ground-floor retail.

The residents received written notice on July 19. They have until September 19 to leave.

Thirty years for $485 a month

The trailer court doesn't look like much from the road. A faded wooden sign marks the entrance. The shells crunch underfoot. Most of the mobile homes date to the 1980s and 1990s, their metal siding streaked with salt and age. But the rents tell a different story.

Hutchins pays $485 a month for her lot. She owns her mobile home outright. Her total housing cost, including utilities and the lease fee she pays to SRIA, runs about $650.

"Show me where else on this island I can live for that," she said. "Show me anywhere in Pensacola Beach."

She's right. A search of available rentals on the island conducted July 20 found no year-round units listed below $1,800 per month. Most one-bedroom apartments near the beach start at $2,200. The median asking rent for a two-bedroom unit in the 32561 ZIP code reached $2,950 in June, according to data from Zillow.

Hutchins survives on Social Security and a small Navy widow's pension. Her combined monthly income is $1,847.

A workforce that can't afford to stay

The twelve households at Via de Luna include a retired electrician, a part-time bartender at Flounders, two housekeepers who clean vacation rentals, and a maintenance worker for one of the large condo associations on the island. Several are over 70. One resident, who asked not to be identified, is undergoing chemotherapy treatment at Baptist Hospital and cannot drive.

None of them have found alternative housing on the island.

"I work here," said Marcus Treadwell, 58, who has cleaned pools and maintained HVAC systems for beachside properties for two decades. "I've lived here nine years. If I move to Pensacola, I'm driving 45 minutes each way. Gas alone eats up what I'd save."

Treadwell's lot rent is $510 a month. He has looked at apartments in Gulf Breeze, Pace, and the West Pensacola corridor. The cheapest option he found—a one-bedroom in Ferry Pass—runs $1,150, does not allow his dog, and would require first and last month's rent plus a security deposit totaling $3,450.

"I don't have that," he said.

The last of its kind

The Via de Luna trailer court is the last remaining mobile home park on Pensacola Beach. In 1985, according to SRIA records reviewed by The Flightline, there were four such parks on the island with a combined 67 lots. The others—Bay Oaks, Islander Village, and Gulf View Trailer Park—were all redeveloped between 1998 and 2012.

The land under the trailer court is owned by the state of Florida and leased to SRIA, which in turn subleases parcels to private developers and residents. The current sublease for the trailer court property has been held since 1979 by Via de Luna Properties LLC, a company originally controlled by a Pensacola family that sold its interest in 2019.

Gulf Coast Development Partners acquired the LLC in a transaction recorded with the Escambia County Clerk on April 3, 2026. The SRIA vote in May approved the associated lease transfer, a procedural requirement for any change in control of subleased island property.

Under the terms of the development agreement, Gulf Coast will pay SRIA $1.2 million in upfront lease consideration plus an annual ground rent of $387,000—roughly eight times what the trailer court generated.

No relocation assistance

The eviction notice sent to residents offers no relocation assistance. Florida law does not require mobile home park owners to compensate displaced tenants unless the park was converted under specific statutes that do not apply to SRIA-controlled land.

At the May 22 SRIA meeting, board member Catherine Calhoun, who cast the lone dissenting vote, asked whether the authority could require Gulf Coast to provide moving assistance or temporary housing subsidies.

"We don't have a mechanism for that," said SRIA executive director Paolo Ghio. "The lease terms don't contemplate it. We'd be adding conditions after the fact."

Calhoun pressed further, asking whether the board had authority to delay the transfer pending a housing impact study.

"Our legal counsel advises that we do not," Ghio said.

The four board members who voted in favor of the transfer—Chairman Randall Wright, Thomas Hightower, Janice Reilly, and Ed Carbone—did not respond to requests for comment.

"Progress" on the beach

Gulf Coast Development Partners describes itself on its website as specializing in "premium Gulf Coast properties that maximize visitor experience and investor returns." The company has developed vacation rental complexes in Destin, Panama City Beach, and Orange Beach, Alabama.

A spokesman for the company, reached by phone on July 20, declined to discuss specifics of the Via de Luna project but provided a written statement.

"Gulf Coast Development Partners is committed to responsible development that enhances the Pensacola Beach community," the statement read. "We are working closely with the Santa Rosa Island Authority to ensure a smooth transition and look forward to bringing new investment and amenities to this premier location."

The statement did not mention the displaced residents.

Nowhere to go

On a Tuesday afternoon, the trailer court is quiet. A few residents sit under awnings, escaping the heat. Someone has taped a hand-lettered sign to the bulletin board near the entrance: "MEETING FRIDAY 6 PM - WHAT DO WE DO NOW?"

Hutchins doesn't know if she'll attend.

"What's there to talk about?" she said. "They made their decision. We weren't part of it."

She has started calling her daughter in Mobile, asking if she can stay there temporarily. Her daughter has two kids and a two-bedroom apartment. There isn't room.

"I keep thinking I'll figure something out," Hutchins said. "But I'm 74. I don't have a car payment because I paid that off in 2018. I don't have a mortgage because I own my trailer. I did everything right. And now I'm going to end up—where? A motel? My daughter's couch?"

She looked out at Via de Luna Drive, at the cars heading toward the beach, at the condominiums rising behind the tree line.

"They want this island to be all tourists," she said. "But who's going to clean the rooms? Who's going to serve the drinks? Not people who can afford to live here. That's for sure."

The wind chimes kept moving. Fifty-nine days left.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's new simulator building breaks ground as Blue Angels pilot shortage continues
articles.dek: The $28 million training facility won't open until 2028. The demonstration squadron has been flying with five jets instead of six since April.
brief: Naval Air Station Pensacola broke ground Monday on a $28 million aviation training simulator facility expected to open in 2028
The Blue Angels have operated with five demonstration pilots instead of six since April due to an ongoing Navy-wide pilot shortage
Base officials say the new facility will help address training backlogs but won't directly solve the demonstration squadron's staffing issues
articles.body:
A yellow excavator bit into the sandy soil Monday morning at the corner of Radford Boulevard and Museum Drive, officially starting construction on a facility Navy officials hope will ease a training crisis that has already touched Pensacola's most visible squadron.

The 45,000-square-foot Naval Aviation Training Systems building will house twelve flight simulators and support equipment for student naval aviators cycling through NAS Pensacola. Rear Admiral James Whitfield, commander of Naval Education and Training Command, called it "a critical investment in the future of naval aviation" during the groundbreaking ceremony attended by roughly 200 people.

What went unmentioned from the podium: the Blue Angels, headquartered a few hundred yards away, have been flying their signature delta formation with five F/A-18 Super Hornets instead of six since April. The demonstration squadron's missing slot—the number 4 position—remains vacant because the Navy cannot spare a qualified pilot from fleet duties.

The pilot math

The Navy has acknowledged a shortage of approximately 1,400 tactical jet pilots across the service. Blue Angels pilots serve two-year tours and must have at least 1,250 flight hours and carrier qualification before joining the team. Those requirements pull from the same pool of experienced aviators needed for operational squadrons.

"We're not in a position to take a fleet pilot and put them in a demonstration billet when the carrier air wings are already short," said Captain Marcus Ellison, commanding officer of NAS Pensacola, in an interview after the ceremony. "It's a hard trade-off, but operational readiness has to come first."

The Blue Angels completed their spring training at NAF El Centro in March with six pilots. By the time the season opened in April at Naval Air Facility El Centro's open house, pilot number 4—traditionally the slot pilot on the right side of the diamond—had been reassigned to a fleet squadron. The Navy has not publicly identified the pilot or explained the specific circumstances of the reassignment.

Blue Angels spokesperson Lieutenant Sarah Chen confirmed the five-jet configuration is expected to continue through the 2026 air show season, which runs through November. "The team has adapted our demonstration to maintain the precision and excitement fans expect," Chen said in a written statement. "Safety remains our top priority."

What the building will do

The new training facility is designed to increase simulator capacity at NAS Pensacola by roughly 40 percent. Currently, student pilots sometimes wait days for simulator slots, a bottleneck that extends their overall training timeline.

Modern flight simulators can replicate nearly every aspect of flight short of actual G-forces. They're cheaper to operate than aircraft, don't require fuel or maintenance crews, and can simulate emergencies that would be too dangerous to practice in real jets.

The building's twelve simulators will include eight for the T-6 Texan II primary trainer and four for the T-45 Goshawk advanced jet trainer. Construction is contracted to Hensel Phelps, the same firm that built the National Naval Aviation Museum's expansion in 2019.

Navy officials projected 6,000 additional simulator hours per year once the facility reaches full operation.

A gap that won't close soon

Even with the new facility, the Navy's pilot shortage isn't expected to stabilize until at least 2030. The service produced roughly 1,100 new pilots last year against annual losses of about 1,300 to retirement, separation, and transfers to other duties.

Pensacola trains approximately 1,500 student naval aviators annually across its various programs. The new simulator building addresses training throughput but doesn't change the fundamental math of retention—pilots leaving for airline jobs that offer better pay, predictable schedules, and no deployments.

A first-year airline captain at a major carrier can earn $350,000 or more. A Navy lieutenant commander with ten years of service makes roughly $120,000 in base pay and benefits.

"You can't simulator your way out of a compensation problem," said Robert Farley, a defense analyst at the University of Kentucky who studies military aviation. "The building helps, but the Blue Angels situation shows where the real pressure point is."

What visitors will see

The Blue Angels' modified routine eliminates certain maneuvers that require six aircraft but preserves the diamond formation, solo performances, and the signature delta roll. Crowds at the team's Pensacola Beach show earlier this month—an estimated 150,000 spectators over two days—showed no signs of diminished enthusiasm.

"Most people can't tell the difference," said Tom Hendricks, who has attended every Pensacola Beach air show since 1992. He was watching the formation pass overhead from the parking lot of the Pensacola Beach RV Resort. "But once you see it, you notice. There's a hole where somebody should be."

The new training facility is expected to open in late 2028. The Blue Angels' 2027 roster has not been announced.
